questions.q: What is the main value of an integration landscape diagram, per this lesson?
options: It replaces the need for an integration inventory entirely
It communicates the shape of a complex, multi-system landscape at a glance, in a way a list of individual integration write-ups can't do as quickly
It is purely decorative and has no practical architecture use
It is only useful for Salesforce-only landscapes with no external systems
questions.explain: A well-made diagram lets a viewer immediately see the shape of an entire integration landscape — which systems connect, how, and how significantly — far faster than reconstructing the same picture from separate documentation for each integration.

questions.q: Which four elements does this lesson say a genuinely useful landscape diagram must show for every connection?
options: Cost, vendor name, contract length, and support tier
Database schema, table names, field types, and index structure
Only the system names, with no other detail needed
The systems involved, direction of data flow, the pattern used, and frequency
questions.explain: A complete diagram labels, for every connection: the systems involved, the direction data flows, the integration pattern used (synchronous, async, batch, event-driven), and the frequency — without these, a diagram is just decorative lines between boxes.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a diagram showing only Salesforce's side of each connection is incomplete?
options: Because the other connected systems (the ERP, the marketing platform, the data warehouse) need to be clearly shown too, or the diagram can't represent the full landscape
Because Salesforce diagrams are never useful for any purpose
Because Salesforce prohibits drawing its own systems in a diagram
Because non-Salesforce systems cannot be represented visually
questions.explain: A landscape diagram's whole purpose is to show the full footprint of connected systems, not just Salesforce's side of each connection — omitting the other systems defeats the purpose of mapping the landscape.

questions.q: In the worked example, why is the bidirectional ERP connection flagged as the most operationally significant link in the diagram?
options: Because it is the oldest connection in the landscape
Because it uses the fewest number of API calls
Because it is bidirectional, near-real-time, and run through shared middleware — a combination that carries more operational weight than a one-way nightly batch link
Because it was the first connection built
questions.explain: The combination of bidirectional flow, near-real-time timing, and shared middleware infrastructure makes the ERP connection carry more operational significance and risk than, for example, a one-way nightly batch feed to a data warehouse.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an outdated, never-updated diagram can be worse than having no diagram at all?
options: Because people stop trusting diagrams entirely once one is found to be outdated
Because people trust it and keep making decisions based on it even as it quietly drifts out of sync with reality, unlike having no diagram, which at least doesn't actively mislead anyone
Because outdated diagrams are illegal to keep on file
Because a diagram automatically deletes itself once it becomes outdated
questions.explain: An outdated diagram is dangerous specifically because people continue to trust and act on it even as new integrations are added or old ones retired without the picture being updated — actively misleading rather than simply absent.
